planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into leafy, well-drained woodland soil in partial to full shade, keeping moisture constant without waterlogging; division builds garden-sized colonies far faster than seed.

directions: Evergreen heart-shaped foliage carries silvery marbling either side of the midrib, and the small purple-brown flowers appear from October into February, blooming when little else is active in the shade garden. Give it the same leafy, well-drained woodland duff you would give a trillium — constant moisture without waterlogging is the main condition for success. Its small stature and winter bloom window make it a good companion planted where you'll walk past it in the cooler months, since the flowers hide at soil level under the leaves.
sources: Plants For A Future (PFAF) / Useful Temperate Plants

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich, neutral-to-acid soil in full to partial shade; it self-sows readily once established, so it can naturalize rather than needing active division.

directions: Dark, unmarked evergreen leaves on a creeping rhizome give this wild ginger a quieter look than the silver-mottled species in the collection, with walnut-colored, mahogany, urn-shaped flowers held tight to the ground. Because it comes from colder central and northern Honshu mountains than many showier Japanese Asarum, it is a reasonable choice for gardeners a zone or two colder than where the most popular Japanese species thrive. Once sited well, let it naturalize rather than forcing division, since it self-sows readily.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into rich, moist woodland soil in dappled to deep shade; seedlings need a full first winter under greenhouse or cold-frame shelter before planting out.

directions: One of the southernmost-adapted Asarum in cultivation, native to mid-elevation subtropical forest in southwest China and northern Vietnam, this species carries purple urn-shaped flowers hidden in the leaf litter that are pollinated by mycotrophic flies. It is a warmer-climate wild ginger than most in the trade, suited to Gulf Coast or Pacific Northwest mild shade gardens rather than colder regions where most Asian species are marketed. Division is slower than seed to produce but far more reliable for building stock.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring under mature trees or with hostas and ferns where summer soil moisture naturally drops; more drought-forgiving than most Asarum once established.

directions: Evergreen leaves with striking random silver 'splats' of marbling set this ginger apart with a more irregular, mottled pattern than other Asian species already in cultivation. It tolerates drier shade than many congeners, making it a useful choice under established trees where summer moisture is unreliable. White flowers with purple centers appear late in the Asarum bloom sequence, after most other wild gingers have finished.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into the richest, most consistently moist woodland soil available; site along a path edge to showcase the unusually large March-April flowers.

directions: A genuine collector-grade addition from Sichuan's wooded slopes, this species carries large, dramatic flowers notably bigger than most garden Asarum, sold by specialty nurseries as rarely available anywhere in the world. Give it the richest, most consistently moist woodland soil available, since Sichuan's wooded slopes are wetter than the drier Japanese hillsides many garden Asarum come from. Its unusually large dark flowers reward close-up viewing in early spring, so site it along a path edge rather than tucked under dense shrub cover.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, rich woodland soil in full shade; treat as a zone 8+ specialty plant or container subject in colder gardens.

directions: One of the largest-leaved Japanese native Asarum, this species carries glossy, unmarked heart-shaped leaves up to 8 inches long on a wide clumping plant, with unusually large pale green, yellow-throated flowers. Its subtropical Ryukyu origin on Amami-Oshima means it is not reliably hardy where mainland Japanese species thrive, so treat it as a zone 8-plus specialty plant or container subject in colder gardens. It is listed as endangered in its native habitat, so source only nursery-propagated stock.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into consistently moist woodland soil in full shade, mimicking its native streamside thicket habitat.

directions: Native to moderate-to-high elevation streamside thickets and moist shaded slopes in Guizhou, Hubei, and Sichuan, this wild ginger gives the collection a distinct interior-China provenance beyond the Japanese and coastal Chinese species already represented. Its streamside, moist-slope origin suggests it wants more consistent moisture than drier-adapted Japanese species grown alongside it. Treat it as a plant for Asarum collectors willing to experiment, since detailed home-garden performance reports are not yet well established.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online
